'Can you check the folder once more?' Karthik asked.
Sabina flipped through it on the hostel common-room table. 'Resume, marksheets, ID. Same as the last three times.'
'Okay. Okay.' He muttered under his breath, 'Good morning, thank you for having me, I'm interested in this role because...'
'You've said that line forty times.'
'What if I blank? What if they ask about the gap semester?'
'Then you tell them what you told me. You were fine.'
'Will you come with me tomorrow? Just sit in the lobby.'
Sabina hesitated. 'I've got a lab at ten.'
'Please. If you're there I'll be calm.' He zipped the folder, then unzipped it to check the ID again. 'See? This is why I need you there.'
Sabina sighed and nodded. Karthik breathed out, and for a minute his shoulders dropped.

qa.q: What does Sabina say is in the folder?
qa.a: The resume, marksheets and ID.

qa.q: What does Karthik believe will happen if Sabina isn't there?
qa.a: He believes he won't be calm without Sabina, as if the interview is only safe with a helper beside him.

qa.q: What could Karthik try at this stage instead of more checking?
qa.a: He could pack the folder once, practise a couple of answers and go alone, letting the nerves rise and fall so he learns he can manage without the safety habits.

qa.q: What is it like for Sabina to be asked to skip the lab?
qa.a: Sabina wants to help but feels torn, and each check and request may leave Sabina tired and unsure whether saying yes really helps him.

grounding: It shows a young man checking, rehearsing and asking a friend to come along, each habit bringing brief calm while confirming the danger.

passage:
Last semester I built a whole system without noticing. Before every class presentation I'd write out every sentence, even the jokes. I'd sit by the door in case I needed to leave. I'd carry two water bottles. And I'd call Gurleen five minutes before, so she could say, 'You'll be fine, Kishore.'
Every time, it worked. I'd get through, sweaty but alive, and think: thank god I did all that.
It took me months to see the trap. I never gave myself the chance to find out I'd have been fine without the script or the call. Every presentation 'proved' that presenting was dangerous and that only my rituals kept me safe.
Last week Gurleen was in a lecture and didn't pick up. I stood outside the room, frozen, thinking: now what?

qa.q: Where would Kishore sit before a presentation?
qa.a: Kishore would sit by the door in case of needing to leave.

qa.q: Why did Kishore feel grateful for the rituals after every presentation?
qa.a: Getting through felt like proof that the script, the water and the call had kept Kishore safe, so the relief got attached to the rituals.

qa.q: What could Kishore try next, now that the trap is visible?
qa.a: Kishore could drop one safety habit at a time, the full script first, and present with the fear, learning that it passes without the ritual.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel on seeing the missed call after the lecture?
qa.a: Gurleen might feel a jolt of worry or guilt, realising how much Kishore had been leaning on that one call.

grounding: It shows someone relying on scripts, an exit seat and a reassuring call, each bringing brief calm but confirming that presenting felt dangerous.

passage:
In their town near Cuttack, Kamal had run the family's small cloth shop since his father fell ill. Every evening he locked the shutter, walked away, then came back to rattle the padlock. Once. Twice. On bad nights, five times, with the tea-stall owner watching.
When he had to go to the post office to send the monthly parcel, he rehearsed his sentences under his breath all the way: "One parcel to Bhubaneswar, registered, please." He made his sister Ira come along, though she had her own college work.
Each time nothing went wrong, and for a moment he felt calm. Then the thought came: it was fine because I checked, because Ira was there. Without that, who knows?
On Friday Ira said, "Bhai, I have an exam. Go alone." Kamal stood at the post office door for ten minutes, rehearsing, heart pounding, before he could make himself step inside.

qa.q: How many times did Kamal rattle the padlock on bad nights?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling at the post office door?
qa.a: He felt anxious and exposed, heart pounding without Ira, because his safety habits had convinced him he couldn't manage alone.

qa.q: What could help Kamal loosen these habits?
qa.a: Check the lock once and walk on, go to the post office without rehearsing every word, and notice that nothing bad happens.

qa.q: What is it like for Ira to be needed everywhere?
qa.a: Ira cares about her brother but feels stretched, torn between her exam and his fears.

grounding: A young shopkeeper rechecks locks, rehearses lines and brings his sister along; each habit calms him briefly but makes the task feel dangerous.

passage:
In his second year at university in Manchester, Emeka had a system. Before every seminar he wrote out his one comment word for word and rehearsed it in the toilets. He always sat by the door. He checked the reading list three times to be sure he hadn't missed anything, and he got Omar, his flatmate, to walk with him to class even though Omar's lectures were in another building.
Each time the seminar went fine, and for a moment he felt calm. Then came the thought: it went fine because I rehearsed, because I sat by the door, because Omar walked me. What if I hadn't?
On Tuesday Omar had a dentist appointment. Emeka stood outside the seminar room with his script, rehearsing, and felt his hands shake. The system that was supposed to protect him now felt like the only thing holding him together.

qa.q: Where did Emeka always sit?
qa.a: By the door.

qa.q: What does Emeka feel when Omar isn't there?
qa.a: He feels shaky and exposed, because his safety habits have taught him the seminar is dangerous without them.

qa.q: What small experiment could Emeka try?
qa.a: Drop one safety habit at a time, like sitting away from the door or speaking without a script, and see that the seminar still goes fine.

qa.q: What might Omar feel about walking Emeka to class?
qa.a: Omar probably cares and wants to help, but may sense the walks are making Emeka rely on him more.

grounding: A student's scripts, checking and escort bring brief calm before seminars but confirm that the situation feels dangerous without them.

passage: The college auditorium was half full for the first-year orientation, and Maria had rehearsed her one-line self-introduction eleven times in the bathroom mirror. She had checked her bag for her ID three times in the corridor. And she had made Shankar, her friend from school, promise to sit next to her. "You'll be right here?" she asked for the second time. "I'm not going anywhere," he said. When her row's turn came, she stood, said her name and course word for word as practised, and sat down fast, breathing out. Relief washed through her. Thank god Shankar was there, she thought. Thank god she'd rehearsed. If she hadn't, she'd have frozen. Afterwards, Shankar mentioned he had a lab on Thursday during her club meeting. Maria's stomach dropped. Then she'd just skip the club, she decided. She couldn't go in alone.

qa.q: How many times had Maria rehearsed her self-introduction in the mirror?
qa.a: Maria had rehearsed it eleven times in the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: Why does Maria feel relief after her introduction?
qa.a: She feels relieved and grateful, but she credits the rehearsing and Shankar's presence, which makes her believe she would have frozen without them.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Maria at this stage?
qa.a: Maria could try the Thursday club meeting alone, maybe with only one rehearsal, to learn that she can cope without her safety habits.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel about being needed everywhere?
qa.a: Shankar may feel caring but also a bit trapped or worried, sensing that his promise has become something Maria cannot manage without.

grounding: Shows a young adult rehearsing, checking and bringing a friend for safety, each habit bringing brief calm but confirming the danger.
